title: Electrons that belong to everyone
question: What holds a metal together if no atom keeps its own outer electrons?
hook: In a metal, the outer electrons stop belonging to any one atom.
idea: Metal atoms release their valence electrons into a shared cloud, and the attraction between the cloud and the positive ions holds the metal together.

beats.prompt: A metal atom gives up its valence electrons to a large delocalized orbital. What is left behind?

choices.label: Negatively charged ions
choices.feedback: It tempts because electrons are moving around, but the atoms are the ones losing electrons, so they end up positive.

choices.label: Neutral atoms with the same electrons as before
choices.feedback: The atoms really do lose their valence electrons into the shared orbital, so they cannot stay neutral.

beats.explain: The nucleus and the electrons closer to it are left as positively charged cations, held together by the negative charge of the delocalized orbital.

beats.prompt: Put these models of metals in the order they developed.
items: Metals as positive ions held by an ocean of electrons
Band structure and density functional models
beats.explain: Electrochemistry gave the ocean-of-electrons picture, quantum mechanics gave the free electron model and its nearly free extension, and the nearly free model's failures led to band structure calculations and density functional theory.

beats.prompt: Match each example to how it relates to metallic bonding.
pairs: Like one molecule with electrons delocalized in three dimensions
Often atomic, or molecules held by a conventional covalent bond
beats.explain: Metals take delocalization to its extreme in two and three dimensions, while in vapours the bonding is more conventional.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about metallic bonding is wrong. Which?
steps: Metal atoms give up valence electrons to a delocalized orbital.
This leaves positively charged ions in a crystal lattice.
The negative charge of the delocalized orbital holds the ions together.
So metallic bonding must be strongly polar, with charge piled on certain atoms.
beats.explain: Metallic bonding is mostly non-polar, because there is little to no difference among the electronegativities of the atoms involved.
